items.content_html:
Follow up from #46088.

The Digital audio concepts guide is needlessly verbose and repeats the same point multiple times (it looks like multiple people went in and added their own self-contained paragraphs without caring about what's already written). It also sketches over important bits about how audio sampling and digitization work. Most importantly the "Psychoacoustics" section has many factually incorrect bits, or at least bits that don't please my linguist's brain. I've rewritten it to IMO be more technically precise and also has a better leadup on the basics of acoustic physics.
items.title: Rewrite Digital audio concepts guide

items.content_html:
Description

Adds a paragraph to "Focusable elements should have interactive semantics" on the Keyboard accessible guide: in browse mode, some screen readers intercept Enter and Space and activate the element with a click event, so keydown and keyup handlers never run. Touch screen readers fire click on double tap. The paragraph tells readers to handle click as well, or use a native <button>. Also adds the click event to the section's "See also" list and fixes "event handlers keyboard events" to "event handlers for keyboard events".

Motivation

The section only recommends keyboard event handlers. A custom control built that way does nothing for an NVDA user in browse mode, which is the case reported in the issue.

Additional details

  • NVDA discussion of the behavior: nvaccess/nvda#7898
  • Checked in Chromium: a focused <button> fires click on both Enter and Space; a focused <div tabindex="0"> gets only keydown and keyup.
  • markdownlint-cli2 and prettier -c pass on the file.

Related issues and pull requests

Fixes #37887
items.title: Keyboard accessible: note that screen readers can replace key events with click

items.content_html:
Description

Adds a reference page for the non-standard console.context() static method under Web/API/console, and lists it on the console interface page.

Motivation

console.context() has shipped in Chrome since version 61 and is also exposed in Node.js, but MDN had no page for it. The page explains what the returned object is, that counters and timers are kept separately for each context, and how the label can be used to filter messages in Chrome DevTools.

Additional details

I checked the behavior in Chrome 154 and Node.js 22:

  • The returned object has 22 console methods (log, warn, count, time, timeStamp, and so on) but no context() of its own, and its methods work without a receiver, including in workers.
  • count("hits") on two different contexts and on console gives three independent counters.
  • In Node.js the messages only reach an attached inspector (with a context field like myLogger#1 in Runtime.consoleAPICalled), nothing is printed to the terminal.

Sources:

  • V8 commit that introduced the method (V8 6.1, so Chrome 61): v8/v8@701d79d08ad4
  • Later V8 change that converts the label with ToString: v8/v8@6b4ed4abb15b
  • DevTools context: filter: https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/devtools-frontend/blob/main/front_end/panels/console/ConsoleFilter.ts
  • Spec proposal: whatwg/console#244 (issue whatwg/console#193)
  • Firefox: https://bugzil.la/1948870, WebKit: https://webkit.org/b/293768, Node.js: nodejs/node#56634

The page is marked non-standard since whatwg/console#244 is still open, and like the other non-standard console pages (profile(), timeStamp()) it has no Specifications section. If the spec PR lands I'm happy to follow up.

Related issues and pull requests

Fixes #46017

Depends on: mdn/browser-compat-data#30814 (adds api.console.context_static)
items.title: Add page for console.context() static method

items.content_html:
Description

In Using readable byte streams, the note in "Underlying push source with byte reader" ends with:

This is similar to the behavior shown in the "pull: underlying byte source examples.

The quote is never closed, and there's no section with that name on the page. This replaces it with links to the two examples that show the behavior the note describes:

This is similar to the behavior shown in the Underlying pull source with default reader and Underlying pull source with default reader and no allocation examples.

Motivation

Readers can't tell which examples the note means, and the unclosed quote reads like a typo.

Additional details

The note is about using a byte source with a default reader, with and without automatic buffer allocation. Those are exactly the two examples linked: the first sets autoAllocateChunkSize, and the second doesn't, so data is enqueued. I'm inferring that these are the intended targets from the content of the note; if you had a different section in mind, I'm happy to change the links.

This sentence has been there since the page was first written in #16818, so I couldn't find an earlier version to go back to. I linked to the sections the same way the page already does elsewhere.

I checked that no other open PR touches this file.

Related issues and pull requests

None.
items.title: Fix the broken reference to examples in Using readable byte streams
